text: In what year was the Consumer Protection Act passed?
explanation: The Consumer Protection Act was passed in 1987, implementing an EU directive on product liability into UK law.

text: What is the primary purpose of the Consumer Protection Act 1987?

options.text: To regulate online shopping and digital downloads
To protect consumers from unsafe products and allow them to claim compensation for damage caused by defective products
To set minimum wage standards for retail workers
To regulate advertising and misleading claims

explanation: The Consumer Protection Act protects consumers from unsafe products and gives them the right to claim compensation for damage caused by defective products — without needing to prove negligence.

text: What is 'strict liability' under the Consumer Protection Act?

options.text: The consumer must prove the producer was negligent
The producer is liable for damage caused by a defective product regardless of whether they were negligent
The retailer is always responsible, not the manufacturer
Liability only applies if the product caused physical injury

explanation: Strict liability means the producer is liable for damage caused by a defective product even if they took all reasonable care — the consumer does not need to prove negligence.

text: Who can be held liable under the Consumer Protection Act for a defective product?

options.text: Only the retailer who sold the product
The producer, importer into the EU, or own-brander of the product
Only the consumer who purchased the product
Only companies with over 50 employees

explanation: Liability under the Act can fall on the producer of the product, the importer who brought it into the EU/UK, or any business that puts their name on the product as an own-brander.

text: How does the Consumer Protection Act apply to software and IT products?

options.text: It does not apply to software — only physical goods
Defective software or IT systems that cause damage or injury could make the producer liable under the Act
Only hardware is covered, not software
It only applies to consumer electronics sold in shops

explanation: The Consumer Protection Act can apply to IT products. Defective software or systems that cause damage — for example a medical system that fails — could expose the producer to liability.

text: What must a consumer prove to make a claim under the Consumer Protection Act?

options.text: That the producer was negligent
That the product was defective, that damage occurred, and that the defect caused the damage
That they purchased the product in the last 30 days
That the product was sold without a warranty

explanation: To claim under the Act a consumer must prove: the product was defective, damage occurred, and the defect caused the damage. They do NOT need to prove negligence.

text: What is a 'defective product' under the Consumer Protection Act?

options.text: Any product that breaks within the first year
A product that does not provide the safety that a person is generally entitled to expect
A product sold without a receipt
Any product that is recalled by the manufacturer

explanation: A product is defective under the Act if it does not provide the safety that a person is generally entitled to expect — taking into account its presentation, purpose and time of supply.

text: What types of damage are covered by the Consumer Protection Act?

options.text: Only physical injury to a person
Death, personal injury and damage to private property over £275
Only damage to the defective product itself
Financial loss caused by the product

explanation: The Act covers death, personal injury and damage to private property over £275. It does not cover damage to the defective product itself or purely financial losses.

text: Why is the Consumer Protection Act relevant to computing professionals who develop safety-critical systems?

options.text: It requires all software to be open source
Defects in safety-critical software — such as medical or aviation systems — that cause injury could result in liability under the Act
It sets coding standards for all software developers
It only applies to hardware engineers

explanation: Computing professionals developing safety-critical systems — such as medical devices or aircraft control software — must be aware that defects causing harm could lead to liability under the Consumer Protection Act.

text: Does the Consumer Protection Act require proof of negligence?

options.text: Yes — negligence must always be proven
No — the Act imposes strict liability so negligence does not need to be proven
Only for products over £500 in value
Only if the damage was to property rather than a person

explanation: The Act imposes strict liability — consumers do not need to prove the producer was negligent, only that the product was defective and caused the damage claimed.

text: What EU directive did the Consumer Protection Act 1987 implement?

options.text: The EU WEEE Directive
The EU Product Liability Directive
The EU General Data Protection Regulation
The EU Digital Single Market Directive

explanation: The Consumer Protection Act 1987 implemented the EU Product Liability Directive into UK law, harmonising product liability rules across EU member states.

text: A development company releases software with a bug that causes a medical device to malfunction, injuring a patient. Which Act is most relevant?

options.text: The Computer Misuse Act 1990
The Consumer Protection Act 1987
The Health and Safety at Work Act 1974
The Digital Economy Act 2010

explanation: The Consumer Protection Act is most relevant here — the defective software caused personal injury, making the producer potentially strictly liable under the Act.

text: What time limit applies to claims under the Consumer Protection Act?

options.text: 1 year from the date of purchase
3 years from when the claimant knew of the damage and defect, with a 10 year longstop
5 years from the date of manufacture
There is no time limit

explanation: Claims must be brought within 3 years of when the claimant knew about the damage and the defect. There is also a 10 year absolute longstop from when the product was first supplied.

text: Can a producer avoid liability under the Consumer Protection Act if the defect was caused by following mandatory government regulations?

options.text: No — strict liability always applies
Yes — compliance with mandatory regulations is one of the available defences
Only if the regulation was passed after the product was made
Only in the medical industry

explanation: Compliance with mandatory government regulations is one of the defences available under the Act — if the defect was required by law, the producer may not be liable.

text: What is the development risks defence under the Consumer Protection Act?

options.text: Producers are not liable if they were a new startup company
Producers may not be liable if the defect could not have been discovered given the state of scientific and technical knowledge at the time
Products under development are exempt from the Act
Open source software is always exempt from liability

explanation: The development risks defence allows producers to avoid liability if they can show the defect could not have been discovered given the state of scientific and technical knowledge at the time the product was supplied.
